doc.title: Carter Benny — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Frank Trumbauer as the inspiration to play saxophone
summary: Hearing Trumbauer's records made him want to play the saxophone and he copied his solos.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Reeds, mouthpieces and horns: the reed player's gear

blocks.x: The personnel of Gene Goldcat’s band at that time supposedly included Bix Beiderbecke and Frankie Trumbauer. Do you remember seeing him?

That’s strange to me, and it must be true, but I don’t know why I wouldn’t remember Frankie Trumbauer and Bix, but especially Trumbauer, because that was the first interest that I heard, or the first playing on record that I heard of a saxophone that made me want to play the instrument, you know, although I went to the trumpet first, but I guess saxophone was sort of my second interest, and it wasn’t hard for me to change from the trumpet, from the weekend trumpet player that I was.
Now, when you first heard him . . . I think this is a good time for a digression on the whole influence of Frankie Trumbauer on leading you to the saxophone. Had you already
switched to taking up an instrument at that point, or had you heard him and that was one of the factors that led you to the saxophone?
It’s hard for me to remember that, but . . .
Because you always cite this at one specific recording.
I Never Miss the Sunshine (I’m So Used to the Rain) by the Don Bestor Orchestra of Chicago [Illinois], or was it somebody else?
Benson Orchestra.
Benson. Benson Orchestra of Chicago.
Right. Now, that was 1923 that was done, so you had to hear it sometime after, in ’23 or later, so I guess . . .
Well, maybe I was already into the saxophone.
You probably would have already been playing.
Yeah. I probably was, but . . .
Maybe that gave you a new direction or something.

Yeah, maybe it gave me something to pattern after, because prior to that I hadn’t . . . gee, I can’t say that I’d heard anybody play the saxophone that really moved me to want to play the instrument, other than just wanting to play the instrument.
What was it about Trumbauer that was different for you?
When you say different, different from what?
Where that made that impression.

Well, I just liked the sound of the horn, the way he played. He had a sort of a almost a delicate touch to him, which I seemed to have heard in later years in Paul Desmond, slightly. Gee, I don’t know how to explain it. I just don’t know how to explain it. But I liked it. I heard him play Singing the Blues, and I think Old-Fashioned Love and a couple of other things, and I started copying his solos from the record.
It was his sound, I guess. Was it his sound or what he was playing or both?

I think both, and he did not play a lot of notes, but he could get over the horn. Every now and then he’d let you know it, you know. [laughter] Yeah. But he had command of the instrument. I liked his approach.
